claim: Social behavior in mammals is often studied in pairs under artificial conditions.
source: Social behavior in mammals is often studied in pairs under artificial conditions, yet groups may rely on more complicated social structures.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context of the manuscript and citations throughout the introduction.

claim: Groups may rely on more complicated social structures than pairs.
source: Social behavior in mammals is often studied in pairs under artificial conditions, yet groups may rely on more complicated social structures.
evidence: This is a foundational claim that motivates the study, supported by the experimental findings presented.

claim: Minimal models that rely only on individual traits and pairwise correlations between animals are not enough to capture group behavior in mice.
source: We have found that the minimal models that rely only on individual traits and pairwise correlations between animals are not enough to capture group behavior, but that models that include third-order interactions give a very accurate description of the group.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the maximum entropy modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Models that include third-order interactions give a very accurate description of group behavior in mice.
source: We have found that the minimal models that rely only on individual traits and pairwise correlations between animals are not enough to capture group behavior, but that models that include third-order interactions give a very accurate description of the group.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis showing that third-order models capture 92.8% ± 2.9% of correlations.

claim: Environmental complexity during adolescence affects the collective group behavior of adult mice.
source: Using this approach, we show that environmental complexity during adolescence affects the collective group behavior of adult mice, in particular altering the role of high-order structure.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison between SE and CE groups shown in Figure 5.

claim: Environmental complexity during adolescence alters the role of high-order structure in group behavior.
source: Using this approach, we show that environmental complexity during adolescence affects the collective group behavior of adult mice, in particular altering the role of high-order structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the differences in contribution of different interaction orders between SE and CE groups.

claim: Insect swarms exhibit coherent collective behavior patterns.
source: The coherence of 'collective behavior' patterns of large groups of animals, such as insect swarms (Buhl et al., 2006; Simpson et al., 2006) fish schools (Sumpter et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2011), bird flocks (Cavagna et al., 2010; Nagy et al., 2010), and human crowds (Song et al., 2010; Gallup et al., 2012), presents us with fundamental questions relating to distributed information processing, computation, and learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on insect swarms.

claim: Fish schools exhibit coherent collective behavior patterns.
source: The coherence of 'collective behavior' patterns of large groups of animals, such as insect swarms (Buhl et al., 2006; Simpson et al., 2006) fish schools (Sumpter et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2011), bird flocks (Cavagna et al., 2010; Nagy et al., 2010), and human crowds (Song et al., 2010; Gallup et al., 2012), presents us with fundamental questions relating to distributed information processing, computation, and learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on fish schools.

claim: Bird flocks exhibit coherent collective behavior patterns.
source: The coherence of 'collective behavior' patterns of large groups of animals, such as insect swarms (Buhl et al., 2006; Simpson et al., 2006) fish schools (Sumpter et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2011), bird flocks (Cavagna et al., 2010; Nagy et al., 2010), and human crowds (Song et al., 2010; Gallup et al., 2012), presents us with fundamental questions relating to distributed information processing, computation, and learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on bird flocks.

claim: Human crowds exhibit coherent collective behavior patterns.
source: The coherence of 'collective behavior' patterns of large groups of animals, such as insect swarms (Buhl et al., 2006; Simpson et al., 2006) fish schools (Sumpter et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2011), bird flocks (Cavagna et al., 2010; Nagy et al., 2010), and human crowds (Song et al., 2010; Gallup et al., 2012), presents us with fundamental questions relating to distributed information processing, computation, and learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on human crowds.

claim: Individual traits may play an important role in shaping group behavior in smaller groups of animals.
source: Smaller groups of animals present an interesting and sometimes more difficult scenario, where individual traits may play an important role in shaping the group behavior (Lathe, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and is a general principle in the field.

claim: Individual behavior and interactions in mammals are often assumed to be more complex than in other animals.
source: This may be especially true in mammals, where both individual behavior and interactions are often assumed to be more complex.
evidence: This is a general assumption in the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Much of our understanding of social behavior has come from studies of just pairs of animals under artificial settings.
source: Yet, much of our understanding of social behavior has come from studies of just pairs of animals under artificial settings (Insel and Fernald, 2004; Langford et al., 2006; Moy et al., 2008; Branson et al., 2009; Dankert et al., 2009; Blumstein et al., 2010; Silverman et al., 2010; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; de Chaumont et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: It is not clear what the detailed analysis of social interaction at the level of a single pair implies for larger groups.
source: It is not clear, however, what the detailed analysis of social interaction at the level of a single pair implies for larger groups.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge in the field.

claim: New features may emerge that characterize the group as a whole that cannot be inferred from the study of individuals or pairs.
source: In particular, new features may emerge that characterize the group as a whole that cannot be inferred from the study of individuals or pairs (Cavagna et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and is a key motivation for the study.

claim: The study analyzed the behavior of 17 groups of mice, each composed of four adult mice.
source: We analyzed the behavior of 17 groups of mice, each composed of four adult mice in an arena resembling an ethologically relevant context that has an interesting environment for exploration (see 'Materials and methods') (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Eight groups of mice were raised in a standard laboratory environment (SE mice).
source: Mice were raised either in a standard laboratory environment (SE mice; eight groups) or an enriched one (CE mice, nine groups; see 'Materials and methods') and studied in the arena using a novel automated system for tracking individual and group behavior simultaneously, with high spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Nine groups of mice were raised in an enriched environment (CE mice).
source: Mice were raised either in a standard laboratory environment (SE mice; eight groups) or an enriched one (CE mice, nine groups; see 'Materials and methods') and studied in the arena using a novel automated system for tracking individual and group behavior simultaneously, with high spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The mice were tracked with high spatial and temporal resolution using a novel automated system.
source: Mice were raised either in a standard laboratory environment (SE mice; eight groups) or an enriched one (CE mice, nine groups; see 'Materials and methods') and studied in the arena using a novel automated system for tracking individual and group behavior simultaneously, with high spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This describes the technical capability of the tracking system used.

claim: The fur of mice was stained with fluorescent hair dyes to enable accurate tracking in the nocturnal phase.
source: To enable accurate tracking of the mice in their nocturnal phase, we stained their fur with fluorescent hair dyes, illuminated the arena with UVA light, and recorded their activity with a sensitive color camera (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for tracking.

claim: The arena was illuminated with UVA light for tracking mice in the dark.
source: To enable accurate tracking of the mice in their nocturnal phase, we stained their fur with fluorescent hair dyes, illuminated the arena with UVA light, and recorded their activity with a sensitive color camera (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for tracking.

claim: The behavior of each group was recorded at 25 frames per second.
source: The behavior of each group was recorded at 25 frames/s, over 4 consecutive nights, for 12 hr each night (Figure 1C and Video 1; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection parameters.

claim: The behavior of each group was recorded over 4 consecutive nights, for 12 hours each night.
source: The behavior of each group was recorded at 25 frames/s, over 4 consecutive nights, for 12 hr each night (Figure 1C and Video 1; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection parameters.

claim: Mice spent much more time in certain locations in the arena.
source: Mice spent much more time in certain locations in the arena (see 'heat map' in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map visualization in Figure 1D.

claim: Individual mice in the group had distinct personal preferences for certain locations.
source: We found that individual mice in the group had distinct personal preferences for certain locations (Figure 1E), and the relative amounts of time spent in different places.
evidence: This is supported by the individual histograms shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The amount of time that each mouse spent continuously at each location had a power-law-like behavior.
source: Despite these individual differences, the amount of time that each mouse spent continuously at each location had a power-law-like behavior (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The power-law distribution of continuous time at locations was similar for different mice.
source: This power-law distribution was similar for the different mice, when they were each analyzed individually, despite their individual differences on other parameters.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of individual mouse behavior.

claim: Out of 10,000 possible states for four mice in 10 zones, only approximately 2000 occurred in the experiment for a typical group.
source: In particular, Figure 2B shows the distribution of observed states for a typical group, where out of the 104 possible states (of 4 mice in 10 zones), only approximately 2000 occurred in the experiment, whereas the independent model predicts that approximately 4000 states would typically occur in our experiment.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The independent model predicts that approximately 4000 states would typically occur in the experiment.
source: In particular, Figure 2B shows the distribution of observed states for a typical group, where out of the 104 possible states (of 4 mice in 10 zones), only approximately 2000 occurred in the experiment, whereas the independent model predicts that approximately 4000 states would typically occur in our experiment.
evidence: This is a prediction from the independent model compared to empirical data.

claim: Correlations between mice contract the space of allowed configurations, such that many of them are socially avoided.
source: In other words, the correlations between mice contract the space of 'allowed' configurations, such that many of them are socially avoided.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference between observed and predicted states.

claim: Knowing the location of one mouse gives relatively little information about the location of another—typically less than 5%.
source: We found that knowing the location of one mouse gives relatively little information about the location of another—typically less than 5% (averaged on all pairs, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mutual information analysis.

claim: The information about the location of one mouse that can be read from the locations of the other mice can be more than double the sum of pairwise information values.
source: Figure 2C shows that this information was highly synergistic—namely that the information about the location of one mouse that can be read from the locations of the other mice can be more than double the sum of pairwise information values of that mouse with all the others: I(xi;xj) + I(xi;xk) + I(xi;xl).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing synergistic information.

claim: The group is not only more complex than a collection of individuals, but much more complex than even the full collection of pairs.
source: Thus, the group is not only more complex than a collection of individuals, but much more complex than even the full collection of pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synergistic information analysis.

claim: The remaining 75% of uncertainty about the location of each mouse is the level of individuality of each mouse, which cannot be explained in terms of the location of the other mice.
source: The remaining 75% of uncertainty about the location of each mouse is exactly the level of individuality of each mouse, which cannot be explained in terms of the location of the other mice.
evidence: This is calculated from the mutual information analysis showing 25% explained by group.

claim: Maximum entropy models from physics can be used to construct minimal models of group behavior based on different orders of dependencies between animals.
source: We therefore used the idea of maximum entropy (ME) models from physics (Jaynes, 1957) to construct minimal models of the group, based on different order of dependencies between the animals.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, supported by citation.

claim: The maximum entropy model is the most parsimonious explanation that does not make any additional assumptions beyond the required features.
source: Since the entropy of a distribution measures its randomness of lack of structure, then among all models that are consistent with some desired feature of the data, the maximum entropy model is the most parsimonious explanation that does not make any additional assumptions beyond the required features.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of maximum entropy models from information theory.

claim: The maximum entropy model is mathematically unique and can be found numerically.
source: This minimal model is mathematically unique and can be found numerically (Schneidman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a mathematical property supported by citation.

claim: Maximum entropy models have been successfully used to infer functional dependencies between neurons, genes, proteins and more.
source: Such models have been successfully used to infer functional dependencies between neurons, genes, proteins and more (e.g., Schneidman et al., 2006; Ganmor et al., 2011; Lezon et al., 2007; Marre et al., 2009; Mora et al., 2010; Stephens et al., 2010; Stephens et al., 2013; Bialek et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The first-order maximum entropy model is exactly the independent model p(1)(x1, x2, x3, x4) = p(x1) p(x2) p(x3) p(x4).
source: The first-order model is one that relies only on the individual behavior of each of the mice, but assumes no dependencies among them at all. The maximum entropy model in this case is built on the observed probability of finding each mouse in one of the regions in the arena, and is exactly the independent model (that we used above), namely p(1)(x1, x2, x3, x4) = p(x1) p(x2) p(x3) p(x4).
evidence: This is a mathematical definition of the first-order model.

claim: The independent model is insufficient to describe the behavior of the group.
source: As it was clear already from Figure 2B, the independent model is insufficient to describe the behavior of the group.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The pairwise model p(2) was a much better model of the group behavior than the independent model, but still shows considerable differences from the empirical data.
source: The top right panel shows that the pairwise model p(2) was a much better model of the group behavior, and captured much of these correlations in the group, but still shows considerable differences from the empirical data.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A top right panel.

claim: The group correlations have a significant higher-order contribution beyond pairwise interactions.
source: The top right panel shows that the pairwise model p(2) was a much better model of the group behavior, and captured much of these correlations in the group, but still shows considerable differences from the empirical data. Thus, the group correlations have a significant higher-order contribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the inadequacy of the pairwise model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The third-order model p(3) gave a very good approximation to the empirical data.
source: We see that p(3) gave a very good approximation to the empirical data (left bottom panel), and was very close to the accuracy of p(4) that relies on all orders of correlations among mice (bottom right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A bottom left panel.

claim: The third-order model p(3) was very close to the accuracy of the fourth-order model p(4).
source: We see that p(3) gave a very good approximation to the empirical data (left bottom panel), and was very close to the accuracy of p(4) that relies on all orders of correlations among mice (bottom right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the bottom panels in Figure 3A.

claim: The comparison of models was performed through cross-validation.
source: We emphasize that the comparison was performed through cross-validation, namely, ME models were fit to a randomly chosen half of the data (train data), and then compared to the empirical distribution based on the other half (test data).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used.

claim: Over all groups, the contribution of the pairwise ME model I(2) was 57.2% ± 10.2% of the total multi-information IN.
source: We found that over all groups, the contribution of the pairwise ME model, given by I(2) was 57.2% ± 10.2% of IN.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the multi-information decomposition.

claim: The third-order contribution I(3) carried nearly a third of the total correlations.
source: We found that I(3) carried nearly a third of the total correlations, and so p(3) that relies on individual traits, pairwise and triple interactions between the mice explains 92.8% ± 2.9% of the correlations (Figure 3B shows as an example the results for the group shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The third-order model p(3) explains 92.8% ± 2.9% of the correlations.
source: We found that I(3) carried nearly a third of the total correlations, and so p(3) that relies on individual traits, pairwise and triple interactions between the mice explains 92.8% ± 2.9% of the correlations (Figure 3B shows as an example the results for the group shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For a group of four mice, using all pairwise interactions is not enough to capture the group behavior.
source: Thus, for a group of four mice even using all pairwise interactions is not enough to capture the group behavior; the third-order interactions are therefore necessary and capture about a third of the correlation structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the multi-information decomposition analysis.

claim: Third-order interactions are necessary to capture group behavior and capture about a third of the correlation structure.
source: Thus, for a group of four mice even using all pairwise interactions is not enough to capture the group behavior; the third-order interactions are therefore necessary and capture about a third of the correlation structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the multi-information decomposition analysis.

claim: The strong high-order dependency is consistent with the synergistic effect seen in the information that can be read about the location of a mouse from that of the other mice.
source: This strong high-order dependency is consistent with the synergistic effect seen in Figure 2 in terms of the information that can be read about the location of a mouse from that of the other mice.
evidence: This connects the multi-information results with the earlier synergy analysis.

claim: The parameters of the maximum entropy models can be interpreted as functional interactions between the mice.
source: The maximum entropy models we have used to describe the group behavior are a generalized form of the Potts model from statistical physics, which describes the behavior of spins in a lattice in terms of the interactions between them (Landau and Lifshitz, 1980). We therefore interpreted the parameters of our ME models as the interactions between the mice at the different locations; these reflect functional (rather than physical) dependencies between the animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the analogy to Potts models from physics.

claim: The functional interactions between mice reflect statistical dependencies rather than physical interactions.
source: We therefore interpreted the parameters of our ME models as the interactions between the mice at the different locations; these reflect functional (rather than physical) dependencies between the animals.
evidence: This clarifies the interpretation of the model parameters.

claim: A regularized third-order maximum entropy model p* is nearly as accurate as the full third-order model but uses far fewer parameters.
source: Specifically, we fitted the maximum entropy model but added a constraint in the form of a cost for every interaction term that is not zero (see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This standard regularization approach gives a model, p*, that is nearly as accurate as the full third model (Figure 4A), but uses far less parameters (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Most pairwise parameters (functional interactions) were negative, making the corresponding configurations less common than predicted from single mouse preferences.
source: We found that most pairwise parameters (or functional interactions) were negative, making the corresponding configurations less common than predicted from single mouse preferences, and positive interactions were less common and weaker, making the corresponding configurations occur more than expected from single mouse traits.
evidence: This is observed from the interaction maps shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Positive interactions were less common and weaker than negative interactions.
source: We found that most pairwise parameters (or functional interactions) were negative, making the corresponding configurations less common than predicted from single mouse preferences, and positive interactions were less common and weaker, making the corresponding configurations occur more than expected from single mouse traits.
evidence: This is observed from the interaction maps shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mere physical limitations do not play a key factor in shaping the group configurations.
source: Importantly, the interaction maps show that mere physical limitations do not play a key factor in shaping the group configurations.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of interaction maps.

claim: The nature of the environment and availability of resources determine population density, aggression, dominance, and territoriality in mice.
source: Since the nature of the environment and availability of resources determine population density, aggression, dominance, and territoriality in mice (Bronson, 1979; Haemisch et al., 1994; Van Loo et al., 2001), we asked how raising mice in a complex and more populated environment (Sztainberg and Chen, 2010; Sztainberg et al., 2010) might affect their group behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on mouse behavior.

claim: CE mice spent significantly more time inside the large nest and less time outside compared to SE mice.
source: We found that groups raised in standard laboratory conditions environment (SE, n = 8) and those raised in a complex environment (CE, n = 9; Figure 5A), already showed distinct behavior at the individual level, as CE mice spent significantly more time inside the large nest and less time outside (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B comparing SE and CE groups.

claim: CE groups were more similar to other CE groups than to SE groups in terms of the overall distribution of observed configurations.
source: We found that CE groups were more similar to other CE groups than to SE groups (and vice versa) in terms of the overall distribution of observed configurations of the mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the similarity matrix in Figure 5C.

claim: The total group correlation IN values of SE and CE groups were similar on the first day.
source: We found that the total group correlation IN values of the SE and CE groups were similar on the first day, but then the SE groups became more correlated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SE groups became more correlated over time.
source: We found that the total group correlation IN values of the SE and CE groups were similar on the first day, but then the SE groups became more correlated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The correlations among CE mice remained unchanged over time.
source: In contrast, the correlations among the CE mice remained unchanged (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was a progressive increase in social correlation, or 'socialization' in the SE groups, which was absent in the CE groups.
source: In other words, there was a progressive increase in social correlation, or 'socialization' in the SE groups, which was absent in the CE groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The differences between SE and CE groups are at the level of group behavior that go beyond the differences between individual behavior patterns.
source: We emphasize that these are differences at the level of group behavior that go beyond the differences between the individual (single animal) behavior patterns of SE and CE mice.
evidence: This emphasizes that the findings are about group-level phenomena.

claim: In CE groups, the contribution of pairwise interaction to the full group correlations was 74.6% ± 2.5%.
source: In the CE groups the contribution of pairwise interaction to the full group correlations was higher than in SE groups (74.6% ± 2.5% in CE groups compared to 61.9% ± 2.4% for the SE ones, averaged over all four days).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the multi-information decomposition.

claim: In SE groups, the contribution of pairwise interaction to the full group correlations was 61.9% ± 2.4%.
source: In the CE groups the contribution of pairwise interaction to the full group correlations was higher than in SE groups (74.6% ± 2.5% in CE groups compared to 61.9% ± 2.4% for the SE ones, averaged over all four days).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the multi-information decomposition.

claim: CE groups showed virtually no contribution of fourth-order interactions.
source: The dominance of the low-order interactions was also reflected by the virtual lack of contribution of fourth-order interaction in the CE groups, whereas the SE groups showed more complex high-order structure (fourth-order interactions contribution to the total correlation in the SE groups was 6.0% ± 0.7% [Figure 5E]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SE groups showed more complex high-order structure with fourth-order interactions contributing 6.0% ± 0.7% to the total correlation.
source: The dominance of the low-order interactions was also reflected by the virtual lack of contribution of fourth-order interaction in the CE groups, whereas the SE groups showed more complex high-order structure (fourth-order interactions contribution to the total correlation in the SE groups was 6.0% ± 0.7% [Figure 5E]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In CE groups, the information from three mice about the fourth was far less synergistic than in SE groups.
source: The larger role of pairwise interactions in shaping the group's behavior is also reflected in the information about the location of one mouse that can be read from the locations of the other three mice. In the CE groups the information from three mice about the fourth was far less synergistic than in the case of SE groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice exposed to a complex environment during adolescence were more individual.
source: Thus, mice exposed to a complex environment during adolescence were more individual, and their weaker group correlations relied more on pairwise rather than higher-order dependencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison of SE and CE groups.

claim: Mice exposed to a complex environment during adolescence had weaker group correlations that relied more on pairwise rather than higher-order dependencies.
source: Thus, mice exposed to a complex environment during adolescence were more individual, and their weaker group correlations relied more on pairwise rather than higher-order dependencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison of SE and CE groups.

claim: Mice are an ideal model organism for investigating social behavior in mammals and the neural mechanisms that underlie it.
source: Mice are an ideal model organism for investigating social behavior in mammals and the neural mechanisms that underlie it.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of mice as a model system.

claim: Mice live in groups and form diverse societies with different characteristics such as group size, hierarchy, aggression, and social tolerance.
source: Together with the ability to manipulate their genomic make-up (Lewandoski, 2001), and record neural activity (electrophysiologically or optically), mice live in groups and form diverse societies with different characteristics such as group size, hierarchy, aggression, and social tolerance (Bronson, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on mouse social behavior.

claim: Current methodologies for analysis of social behavior in mice have focused mainly on dyadic interactions.
source: However, despite the complex nature of their social organization, the current methodologies used for analysis of social behavior in mice have focused mainly on dyadic interactions such as in the classical three-chamber social approach test and the partition test (Silverman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current methods, supported by citation.

claim: The tracking system enables automatic tracking of group behavior of mice in the dark, over long periods of time, and in a semi-natural environment, with high spatiotemporal resolution while maintaining individual identities.
source: The system we introduce here enables automatic tracking of group behavior of mice in the dark, over long periods of time, and in a semi-natural environment, with high spatiotemporal resolution while maintaining individual identities.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the tracking system developed.

claim: RFID-based systems allow for tracking of a very large number of animals.
source: We note that RFID-based systems allow for the tracking of a very large number of animals, whereas our tracking capacity depends on the number of distinguishable dyes and spatial marking patterns on the mice (our preliminary results suggest we can expand even the current system to more than 10 mice).
evidence: This compares the current system to RFID-based alternatives.

claim: The strength of the current tracking system is in its much higher spatial and temporal resolution compared to RFID-based systems.
source: However, the strength of our system is in its much higher spatial and temporal resolution, and the ability to track and analyze details of individual behavior of the animals and between them.
evidence: This describes the advantages of the current system.

claim: Freund et al. showed correlation between the roaming behavior of a mouse and the level of neurogenesis in its hippocampus.
source: The recent work by Freund et al. used the tracking of many mice over several months to study the individual mouse behavior within a large group and showed correlation between the roaming behavior of a mouse and the level of neurogenesis in its hippocampus (Freund et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited work.

claim: The pairwise-based model of the group could only explain approximately 60% of the correlation structure in the group.
source: Intriguingly, the pairwise-based model of the group that assumed no higher-order contribution could only explain approximately 60% of the correlation structure in the group, whereas models that included also third-order dependencies (but not fourth-order ones) captured approximately 90% of the group correlation structure.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative findings from the multi-information analysis.

claim: Models that included third-order dependencies captured approximately 90% of the group correlation structure.
source: Intriguingly, the pairwise-based model of the group that assumed no higher-order contribution could only explain approximately 60% of the correlation structure in the group, whereas models that included also third-order dependencies (but not fourth-order ones) captured approximately 90% of the group correlation structure.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative findings from the multi-information analysis.

claim: Three-quarters of the uncertainty about the location of a mouse comes from its own individuality.
source: That is, the mice still have a significant individual component, even given the other mice.
evidence: This is calculated from the 25% of information explained by other mice.

claim: Most social behaviors, such as fights, chases, courtship, and grooming, are usually observed in pairs.
source: The need for models that include high-order interactions is surprising, since intuitively one might have expected that it would be possible to construct a mathematically accurate description of the group once all the interactions between pairs of mice were known. After all, most social behaviors, such as fights, chases, courtship, and grooming, are usually observed in pairs.
evidence: This is a general observation about social behaviors.

claim: In almost all cases of biological networks studied with maximum entropy models, the contribution of pairwise interactions was very large and dominated the network structure, especially in small networks.
source: Interestingly, in almost all these cases the contribution of pairwise interactions was very large and dominated the network structure, especially in small networks—in clear contrast to what we found for the mice.
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior work on other biological systems.

claim: The findings for mice are in clear contrast to other biological networks where pairwise interactions dominate.
source: Interestingly, in almost all these cases the contribution of pairwise interactions was very large and dominated the network structure, especially in small networks—in clear contrast to what we found for the mice.
evidence: This highlights the novelty of the findings.

claim: The functional interactions reflect statistical dependencies and will probably differ from explicit physical interactions between the animals.
source: We emphasize that these functional interactions reflect statistical dependencies, and will probably differ from explicit physical interactions between the animals that one could measure.
evidence: This clarifies the interpretation of the model parameters.

claim: The statistical dependencies highlight the most prominent relations that underlie the patterns of group behavior.
source: Yet, these statistical dependencies highlight the most prominent relations that underlie the patterns of group behavior.
evidence: This explains the utility of the functional interaction analysis.

claim: The strongest functional interactions corresponded not to the most frequent events, but rather to those events that are most surprising or not predicted from lower orders of interactions.
source: The strongest functional interactions corresponded not to the most frequent events, but rather to those events that are most surprising or not predicted from lower orders of interactions, thus presenting interactions of a truly social nature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction parameters.

claim: The dominant interactions in the group are negative ones, namely compound configurations that tend not to happen compared to expectations based on individual behavior.
source: Our results show that the dominant interactions in the group are negative ones, namely compound configurations that tend not to happen compared to expectations based on individual behavior.
evidence: This is observed from the interaction maps in Figure 4.

claim: The dominance of negative interactions may suggest competition as a dominant force in the social structure.
source: This may suggest competition as a dominant force in the social structure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the negative interactions.

claim: The relative sparseness of the interaction maps indicates that even a small number of social events can have a strong, macroscopic impact on the group.
source: In addition, the relative sparseness of the interaction maps indicates that even a small number of social events can have a strong, macroscopic impact on the group.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sparse interaction structure.

claim: The arena consisted of a 70 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm cage.
source: The arena consisted of an open 70 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm box and included the following objects: Z-shaped wall, a water dispenser, two feeders, a small nest and a large nest, an elevated block, and two elevated ramps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the physical setup of the arena.

claim: Adult male ICR mice from Harlan Laboratories were used for the standard and complex environment experiment.
source: Adult male ICR mice (Harlan Laboratories, Jerusalem, Israel) were used for the standard and complex environment experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: The raw camera acquisition rate was 25 frames per second (40 ms per frame).
source: The raw camera acquisition rate was 25 frames/s (40 ms per frame).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: In analyzing the configurations of the mice, a lower resolution of 240 ms per frame was used.
source: In analyzing the configurations of the mice we used a lower resolution of 240 ms per frame, as this did not have a major effect on the state distribution, but was more robust to single frame noise.
evidence: This describes the data processing approach.

claim: Validation of the tracking algorithm gave 99.6% accuracy compared to human labeling.
source: Validation of the tracking algorithm was performed by comparing the algorithm's performance to human labeling of 500 randomly chosen frames, which gave 99.6% accuracy.
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result.
